title: Two bishops: the wall and the corner
summary: Bishops side by side shut the door; the king pushes all the way to a corner.
part.mates.title: Bishops side by side
part.mates.summary: The two bishops' wall and the two mating patterns.
part.edge.title: Driving the king to the corner
part.edge.summary: The bishops push, the king follows, and the black king ends up in the corner.
part.finish.title: Stalemate and full games
part.finish.summary: The move that draws near the corner, the rules, and the mate from start to finish.
step.t_wall: The two bishops stand side by side in the center. Which squares do they take from the black king, and what is the plan to take it to mate?
step.t_wall.hint1: Follow the bishops' four diagonals and mark the squares they take. Then think about who needs to help them.
step.wall: You already gave this mate in my school. Now let's understand why it works. Look at the bishops on d5 and e5, side by side. One moves on the light squares, the other on the dark ones, and their diagonals cross like an X. The black king on d7 is locked in a small strip: c8, d8, e8, f8, d7 and e7. He cannot cross those diagonals. That is the wall. Notice that it stands without any help from the white king: the king comes later, to push.
step.mateCorner: Where are we taking the black king? To a corner. This is the mate we are after: black king on h8, your king on g6 takes g7 and h7, the bishop on e6 takes g8, and the bishop on e5 gives check along the long diagonal. The bishops finish side by side, just as they started. The wall becomes the mate. And here is good news: with two bishops, any corner will do. In the bishop and knight mate only the corner of the bishop's colour works; here you have one bishop of each colour.
step.mateSide: There is a second picture, on the square next to the corner. Black king on b8, your king on b6, the light bishop on b7, protected by the king and taking a8 and c8, and the dark bishop giving check from d6. Reuben Fine, back in 1941, showed that the mate can only be forced in the corner or right beside it. In the middle of the edge the king always slips out through one square. So the edge is only the first stop; the destination is the corner.
step.join: Back to the wall. The black king is locked at the top of the board, but locked is not beaten. Now bring your king. It does not walk through the wall: it goes around the side and stands in front of the bishops, face to face with the black king. Two king moves.
step.join.hint: The white king climbs the f-file, next to the bishop on e5, and then steps onto the sixth rank, facing the black king.
step.join.done: Kf5 and Ke6. Now your king takes d7, e7 and f7, and the bishops do the rest. The black king went to d8: he is on the edge now and will not come back.
step.edge: The black king is on the edge, on d8. Now the wall steps down to push him towards a corner. First the light bishop takes c8, so the king cannot run towards a8. Then the dark bishop takes d8. Two bishop moves, and the black king will have only one way to go.
step.edge.hint: The light bishop goes to the a8–h1 diagonal, to a square that covers c8. After the king goes to e8, the dark bishop goes to c7.
step.edge.done: Bb7 and Bc7. Now the black king only has f8: he is being pushed towards h8. The bishops work from a distance, and your king will follow.
step.corner: The black king on f8 tries to breathe. Your king follows along the sixth rank; when the black king goes back to e8, a bishop check sends him back; and the light bishop settles on d7, where it takes e8 for good. Three moves.
step.corner.hint: First Kf6, no hurry. If the black king goes to e8, Bc6+ forces Kf8. Then the light bishop goes from c6 to d7.
step.corner.done: Kf6, Bc6+ and Bd7. Now the black king only has f8, g8 and h8. The box is almost shut.
step.mate: Time to mate. Your king goes to g6. The black king chooses f8. Then check with the dark bishop on d6, check with the light bishop on e6, and the dark bishop closes on e5. Four moves, and the last three are all bishop moves.
step.mate.hint: Kg6 first. With the black king on f8: Bd6+, he goes to g8; Be6+, he goes to h8; and the bishop on d6 steps onto the long diagonal.
step.mate.done: Checkmate. King on g6, bishops on e5 and e6, side by side. It is the picture from the start of the lesson.
step.waiting: And what if, after Kg6, the black king had gone to h8 instead of f8? Look: he only has g8. If you check now, he runs; if the light bishop takes g8 without check, it is stalemate and a draw. The right thing is to wait. Move the dark bishop to a square that changes nothing, the black king has to go to g8, and then the checks come.
step.waiting.hint: The dark bishop goes to d6: no check, it does not take g8, and from there it reaches e5 at the right moment. After Kg8, check with the light bishop on e6.
step.waiting.done: Bd6, Be6+ and Be5 mate. A move that did nothing was the most important move. The waiting move is your weapon against stalemate.
step.t_stalemate: The black king is in the corner, held by the bishops and our king. Before moving: which natural move here would throw the win away?
step.t_stalemate.hint1: Count the black king's squares after each of your moves. If none is left and there is no check, it is a draw.
step.stalemate: Stalemate is the only way to throw this ending away. Jeremy Silman shows this position. The black king is on a8 and only has a7. Kb6 looks natural: the white king comes closer. But Kb6 takes a7, and the black king has no move at all while not in check. Stalemate, a draw. Rule: near the corner, before every move, count the black king's squares. If only one is left, your next move is either checkmate or leaves that square free.
step.rules: Three rules to take to your games. First: bishops side by side, near the centre, make a wall the king cannot cross. Second: your king goes in front of the bishops and pushes; the bishops step down one at a time, taking the black king to the edge and then to a corner, any corner. Third: near the corner, count the black king's squares; if he has only one, wait with a bishop instead of stalemating. Now it is your turn.
step.playWall: The whole wall position, against the machine. It will not follow the lesson: it will look for the most stubborn defence. Keep the wall, bring your king and take the black king to any corner.
step.playCenter: Now from the start, with the pieces at home. This is the position Yasser Seirawan uses to teach the mate. First the king leaves home and the bishops come to the centre, side by side. Then the road you already know.
ex.e01: White to play and mate. The black king is on h8 and has no squares at all. Careful: almost every move is stalemate.
ex.e01.hint: The black king has no move, so only a check will do. Which bishop can reach the long diagonal?
ex.e01.solution: Be5 is mate: the dark bishop checks along the a1–h8 diagonal, the bishop on c4 takes g8, and your king takes g7 and h7. Any move without check would have stalemated the black king.
ex.e02: White to play and mate. The black king is on b8, next to the corner, also without squares.
ex.e02.hint: The light bishop on b7 already takes a8 and c8. The check is missing, and it has to come along the dark squares.
ex.e02.solution: Bd6 is mate: the check comes from d6, along the diagonal to b8; c7 is covered too. It is the second mating picture, on the square next to the corner. Any other dark-bishop move without check would have been stalemate.
ex.e03: White to play and win. The black king is on c1, on the edge, and the bishops have already taken nearly the whole board from him. One last gap needs closing.
ex.e03.hint: There is still one square on the second rank where the black king can climb out. Your king can take it without losing contact.
ex.e03.solution: Kc3. Your king takes b2, c2 and d2, and the black king can only walk along the first rank. It is the same move as Kf6 in the lesson, seen from below: no other move keeps the pace.
ex.e04: White to play and win. The black king is on h8 and only has h7. There is a natural move that draws. Find one that wins.
ex.e04.hint: Taking h7 with the light bishop leaves the black king with no move and no check. Before that, give a check or wait with the dark bishop.
ex.e04.solution: Bg7+ forces Kh7, and then Bd3 is mate: the bishop on g7, protected by your king, takes h6 and h8. A waiting move with the dark bishop, or Kg6, also wins. What you cannot play is Bd3 right now: stalemate.
ex.e05: White to play and win. The black king on h8 only has g8. Do not stalemate him and do not let him breathe.
ex.e05.hint: You need to pass the move. The dark bishop can move without check and without taking g8, and stay close to the long diagonal.
ex.e05.solution: Bd6 (or Bf4) is the waiting move. The black king goes to g8, Be6+ sends him back to h8, and Be5 is mate. Be6 now would be stalemate, and so would Kf7.
ex.e06: White to play and win. The black king is on c1, and the nearest corner is a1. Three moves, all with bishops.
ex.e06.hint: A check with the dark bishop moves the king off his square; a check with the light bishop takes him to the corner; the dark bishop closes on the long diagonal.
ex.e06.solution: Be3+ Kb1, Bd3+ Ka1, Bd4 mate. It is the end of the lesson, seen in the bottom corner: the bishops finish side by side on d3 and d4.
ex.e07: White to play and win. The black king is on d8, on the edge. Send him to the a8 corner.
ex.e07.hint: Take e8 from the black king with the light bishop; he can then only walk towards a8. Then your king follows.
ex.e07.solution: Bf7 takes e8, and the black king goes to c8. Then Kc6 takes b7, c7 and d7: the black king stays on the eighth rank with no way back to the centre, and the next job is to take him to a8. Other light-bishop moves (Bc6, Be4, Bf3) also keep the pace, but Bf7 is the clearest.
ex.e08: White to play and win. The bishops stand side by side on d4 and e4, and the black king is on c1, on the edge. Bring your king and start pushing.
ex.e08.hint: Your king goes in front of the bishops, facing the black king. Then the dark bishop takes c1 along the long diagonal.
ex.e08.solution: Ke3 Kd1, Bb2: the dark bishop takes c1 and a1, and the black king only has e1, heading for the h1 corner. It is the same idea as Ke6 and Bb7 in the lesson. Other bishop moves also keep the pace, but this one shuts the a1 side.
ex.e09: White to play and win. The black king is on g8 and wants f8 and h8. Shut the box without stalemate and give mate. Four moves.
ex.e09.hint: First take f8 with the dark bishop, without check. When the king goes to h8, your king steps up to g6. Then a light-bishop check and the mate on the long diagonal.
ex.e09.solution: Bd6 takes f8 and the black king goes to h8. Kg6, and he only has g8. Bd5+ (the light bishop checks along the a2–g8 diagonal) Kh8, and Be5 mate.
ex.e10: White to play and win. The black king is on a5, on the a-file. Drive him towards the a1 corner. Three moves.
ex.e10.hint: The light bishop shuts a6 from the long diagonal, the dark bishop shuts a5, and your king comes down with them.
ex.e10.solution: Bb7 Ka4, Bb6 Ka3, Kc3. The wall came down one step at a time and the white king followed: the black king is stuck between a2 and a4, with no way to the centre. It is the road of the lesson, turned around on the board.
ex.e11: White to play and win. The black king is on g4, to the right of the wall. Bring your king in front of the bishops and push the black king onto the h-file. Three moves.
ex.e11.hint: The white king walks around the wall and stands facing the black king. Then the light bishop shuts the way down.
ex.e11.solution: Ke6 Kh3, Kf5 Kh4, Bg2. The black king is stuck between h4 and h5: g3 belongs to the dark bishop, g4 and g5 to your king, h3 to the light bishop. Now he can only go up, towards h8.
key.wall: The wall: bishops side by side on d5 and e5. The black king is locked at the top of the board. Lesson position.
key.mateCorner: The corner mate, with the bishops side by side. One of the two mating pictures that can be forced (Fine, 1941, via Wikipedia).
key.mateSide: The mate next to the corner: light bishop on b7 protected by the king, check from d6. The other picture that can be forced (Fine, 1941, via Wikipedia).
key.stalemate: Silman's stalemate trap: Kb6?? takes the black king's last square, without check.
key.seirawan: Seirawan's position, with the pieces at home: black king on d4. The book takes the king to the edge and the corner, and the tablebase finds even shorter roads.
history: The bishops never needed a famous discoverer: this mate is in almost every endgame book. Reuben Fine, in Basic Chess Endings (1941), already described the mating pictures and warned that two bishops of the same colour can never mate, not even nine of them. Müller and Lamprecht, in Fundamental Chess Endings (2001), show that with the bishops to move the mate fits comfortably inside the fifty-move rule; Speelman, Tisdall and Wade point out the very rare exceptions. Authors disagree on whether it is worth studying: James Howell left the bishop mate out of his book because it almost never happens; Jeremy Silman did the opposite, teaching the bishops and leaving out the bishop and knight mate. And Fred Reinfeld said that the road, a little long, shows like few others the power of the bishop pair on an open board.
practice: Now the real ending. The black king is in the centre and your bishops are still far apart. Bring the bishops together, bring your king, and take the black king to a corner without stalemating. Choose the time control and race the clock, or set up your own training.
